title: Decision Tree
content:
A decision tree is a tree-shaped classification model in which every internal node tests one attribute of the input, every branch represents the outcome of that test, and every leaf node assigns a class label. To classify a new example, start at the root and follow the branch matching the example's attribute values, node after node, until a leaf is reached.

This is nothing more than a nested sequence of if-else questions applied to the attributes of an example.

title: Example 2.1 --- Classifying an Instance from a Cricket Tree
content:
The table below shows whether Ali played cricket based on the weather.
| \toprule Weather | Temperature | PlayCricket |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Sunny | Hot | No |
| Sunny | Cold | Yes |
| Rainy | Hot | Yes |
| Rainy | Cold | Yes |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
The decision tree built from this data is shown below.

Use this tree to classify a new instance: Weather = Sunny Temperature = Cold.

Solution:
Start at the root. Weather = Sunny, so move to the Temperature node. Temperature = Cold, so move to the right branch, which is a leaf labeled Yes. \\
Predicted class: \boxed{\text{Yes}}

title: Decision Tree Terminology: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Root node
content:
Decision Tree Terminology:

1. Root node the topmost node where classification always begins
2. Internal node a node that tests one attribute and branches on its values
3. Branch (edge) represents one possible value of the tested attribute
4. Leaf node a terminal node that outputs a class label with no further test

\subsection{Entropy and Impurity}

title: Entropy
content:
For a set $S$ containing examples from $c$ classes, entropy measures how mixed or impure the set is:
\[
H(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \log_2 p_i
\]
where $p_i$ is the proportion of examples in $S$ belonging to class $i$.

This is the same weighted-average-of-surprise idea used in information theory.

title: Properties of Entropy
content:
1. $H(S) = 0$ when every example in $S$ belongs to the same class \hfill(pure set)
2. $H(S)$ is largest when the classes are split as evenly as possible \hfill(maximum impurity)
3. $0 \le H(S) \le \log_2 c$ for a set with $c$ classes \hfill(bounds)

title: Example 2.4 --- Entropy of a Mixed Exam Result Set
content:
A dataset $S$ of 6 students contains 4 examples labeled Pass and 2 examples labeled Fail. Compute $H(S)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
p(\text{Pass}) &= \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad p(\text{Fail}) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3} \\
H(S) &= -\frac{2}{3}\log_2\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\log_2\frac{1}{3} \\
&= -\frac{2}{3}(-0.585) - \frac{1}{3}(-1.585) \\
&= 0.390 + 0.528
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{H(S) \approx 0.918}

title: Example 2.5 --- Entropy of a Pure Fruit Set
content:
A dataset $S$ of 5 fruits contains 5 examples all labeled Mango. Compute $H(S)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
p(\text{Mango}) &= \frac{5}{5} = 1 \\
H(S) &= -(1)\log_2(1) = -(1)(0)
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{H(S) = 0}
Since every example belongs to one class, the set is completely pure, matching Property 1 above. ✓

title: Example 2.6 --- Entropy of a Balanced Coin Toss Set
content:
A dataset $S$ of 6 coin tosses contains 3 examples labeled Heads and 3 examples labeled Tails. Compute $H(S)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
p(\text{Heads}) &= \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}, \qquad p(\text{Tails}) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2} \\
H(S) &= -\frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{2} \\
&= -\frac{1}{2}(-1) - \frac{1}{2}(-1) \\
&= 0.5 + 0.5
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{H(S) = 1}
This is the largest possible entropy for a two-class set, matching Property 2 above. ✓

title: Quick Reference: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] $_2 2 =
content:
Quick Reference:

1. $\log_2 2 = 1$ and $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ (values needed for almost every entropy calculation in this chapter)
2. $H(S) = 0$ means pure and $H(S) = 1$ means maximum impurity for a two-class set
3. Lower entropy is always better for building compact decision trees

\subsection{Information Gain}

title: Information Gain
content:
Information Gain measures how much entropy is reduced by splitting a set $S$ on attribute $A$:
\[
\text{Gain}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_{v \in Values(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v)
\]
where $S_v$ is the subset of $S$ for which attribute $A$ has value $v$.

Think of it as the total entropy minus a weighted average of the entropies of the resulting pieces.

title: Example 2.7 --- Information Gain of Weather
content:
Consider the dataset below.
| \toprule Weather | Temperature | PlayCricket |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Sunny | Hot | No |
| Sunny | Cold | No |
| Sunny | Hot | Yes |
| Rainy | Cold | Yes |
| Rainy | Cold | Yes |
| Rainy | Hot | Yes |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
Compute $\text{Gain}(S,\text{Weather})$.

Solution:
The set has 4 Yes and 2 No, the same proportion as Example 2.4, so $H(S) \approx 0.918$.
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Sunny}} &= \{\text{No,No,Yes}\}: \ 1 \text{ Yes}, 2 \text{ No} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Sunny}}) \approx 0.918 \\
S_{\text{Rainy}} &= \{\text{Yes,Yes,Yes}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Rainy}}) = 0 \\
\text{Weighted entropy} &= \frac{3}{6}(0.918) + \frac{3}{6}(0) = 0.459 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Weather}) &= 0.918 - 0.459
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Gain}(S,\text{Weather}) \approx 0.459}

title: Example 2.8 --- Information Gain of Temperature
content:
Using the same dataset as Example 2.7, compute $\text{Gain}(S,\text{Temperature})$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Hot}} &= \{\text{No,Yes,Yes}\}: \ 2 \text{ Yes}, 1 \text{ No} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Hot}}) \approx 0.918 \\
S_{\text{Cold}} &= \{\text{No,Yes,Yes}\}: \ 2 \text{ Yes}, 1 \text{ No} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Cold}}) \approx 0.918 \\
\text{Weighted entropy} &= \frac{3}{6}(0.918) + \frac{3}{6}(0.918) = 0.918 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Temperature}) &= 0.918 - 0.918
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Gain}(S,\text{Temperature}) = 0}
Since Gain(Weather) $\approx 0.459 >$ Gain(Temperature) $= 0$, Weather is the better attribute to split on first.

title: Example 2.9 --- Information Gain of Sky Condition
content:
Consider a dataset about carrying an umbrella.
| \toprule Sky | Humidity | TakeUmbrella |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Cloudy | High | Yes |
| Cloudy | Low | Yes |
| Cloudy | High | Yes |
| Clear | Low | No |
| Clear | Low | No |
| Clear | High | Yes |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
Compute $\text{Gain}(S,\text{Sky})$.

Solution:
The set has 4 Yes and 2 No, so $H(S) \approx 0.918$.
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Cloudy}} &= \{\text{Yes,Yes,Yes}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Cloudy}}) = 0 \\
S_{\text{Clear}} &= \{\text{No,No,Yes}\}: \ 1 \text{ Yes}, 2 \text{ No} \Rightarrow H(S_{\text{Clear}}) \approx 0.918 \\
\text{Weighted entropy} &= \frac{3}{6}(0) + \frac{3}{6}(0.918) = 0.459 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Sky}) &= 0.918 - 0.459
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Gain}(S,\text{Sky}) \approx 0.459}

title: Choosing the Splitting Attribute: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Compute
content:
Choosing the Splitting Attribute:

1. Compute $H(S)$ for the current set
2. Compute the weighted entropy after splitting on each candidate attribute
3. The attribute with the highest Information Gain is chosen for the node
4. An attribute giving Gain $= 0$ tells us nothing new about the class, so it is never chosen over a better one

\subsection{The ID3 Algorithm}

title: ID3 Algorithm
content:
Input: A set of training examples $S$ a target class attribute and a set of candidate attributes $A$

Output: A decision tree that classifies the training examples

1. Create a root node for the tree.
2. If all examples in $S$ belong to the same class $c$ label the root with $c$ and stop.
3. If the attribute set $A$ is empty label the root with the majority class in $S$ and stop.
4. Otherwise compute Information Gain for every remaining attribute in $A$ and select the attribute $A^\ast$ with the highest gain as the decision attribute for the root.
5. For each possible value $v$ of $A^\ast$ add a new branch below the root for $A^\ast = v$ and let $S_v$ be the subset of examples with $A^\ast = v$.
6. If $S_v$ is empty attach a leaf labeled with the majority class of $S$ below this branch.
7. Otherwise attach the subtree obtained by recursively applying steps 2 to 6 to $S_v$ using $A - \{A^\ast\}$ as the remaining attribute set.
8. Return the root node.

title: Example 2.10 --- Building a Tree for the Walk Dataset
content:
Build the ID3 decision tree for the dataset below.
| \toprule Weather | Wind | Walk |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Sunny | Weak | Yes |
| Sunny | Weak | Yes |
| Sunny | Strong | Yes |
| Rainy | Weak | No |
| Rainy | Weak | No |
| Rainy | Strong | No |
| \bottomrule |  |  |

Solution:
The set has 3 Yes and 3 No, so $H(S) = 1$ (Example 2.6 pattern).
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Sunny}} &= \{\text{Yes,Yes,Yes}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
S_{\text{Rainy}} &= \{\text{No,No,No}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Weather}) &= 1 - \left[\frac{3}{6}(0) + \frac{3}{6}(0)\right] = 1
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Weak}} &= \{\text{Yes,Yes,No,No}\}: \ 2/2 \Rightarrow H = 1 \\
S_{\text{Strong}} &= \{\text{Yes,No}\}: \ 1/1 \Rightarrow H = 1 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Wind}) &= 1 - \left[\frac{4}{6}(1) + \frac{2}{6}(1)\right] = 0
\end{align*}$$
Since Gain(Weather) $= 1 >$ Gain(Wind) $= 0$, Weather is chosen as the root. Both resulting subsets are already pure, so ID3 stops immediately (step 2).

\boxed{\text{Final Tree: Weather} \to \{\text{Sunny}: \text{Yes}, \ \text{Rainy}: \text{No}\}}

title: Example 2.11 --- Building a Tree for Loan Approval
content:
Build the ID3 decision tree for the dataset below.
| \toprule Income | CreditScore | LoanApproved |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule High | Good | Approve |
| High | Bad | Approve |
| High | Bad | Approve |
| Low | Good | Approve |
| Low | Bad | Deny |
| Low | Bad | Deny |
| \bottomrule |  |  |

Solution:
The set has 4 Approve and 2 Deny, so $H(S) \approx 0.918$.
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{High}} &= \{\text{Approve,Approve,Approve}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
S_{\text{Low}} &= \{\text{Approve,Deny,Deny}\}: \ 1/3, 2/3 \Rightarrow H \approx 0.918 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Income}) &= 0.918 - \left[\frac{3}{6}(0) + \frac{3}{6}(0.918)\right] = 0.459
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Good}} &= \{\text{Approve,Approve}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
S_{\text{Bad}} &= \{\text{Approve,Approve,Deny,Deny}\}: \ 2/2 \Rightarrow H = 1 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{CreditScore}) &= 0.918 - \left[\frac{2}{6}(0) + \frac{4}{6}(1)\right] = 0.251
\end{align*}$$
Since Gain(Income) $\approx 0.459 >$ Gain(CreditScore) $\approx 0.251$, Income is chosen as the root.
Income = High is already pure (Approve). Income = Low is not pure and must be split further using the only remaining attribute, CreditScore:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Low, Good} &\to \{\text{Approve}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow \text{leaf } = \text{Approve} \\
\text{Low, Bad} &\to \{\text{Deny,Deny}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow \text{leaf } = \text{Deny}
\end{align*}$$

\boxed{\text{Final Tree: Income} \to \{\text{High}: \text{Approve}, \ \text{Low} \to \text{CreditScore} \to \{\text{Good}: \text{Approve}, \text{Bad}: \text{Deny}\}\}}

title: Example 2.12 --- Building a Tree for Exam Result Prediction
content:
Build the ID3 decision tree for the dataset below.
| \toprule Study | Sleep | Result |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Yes | Enough | Pass |
| Yes | Enough | Pass |
| Yes | Little | Pass |
| No | Enough | Fail |
| No | Enough | Fail |
| No | Little | Pass |
| \bottomrule |  |  |

Solution:
The set has 4 Pass and 2 Fail, so $H(S) \approx 0.918$.
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Study=Yes}} &= \{\text{Pass,Pass,Pass}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
S_{\text{Study=No}} &= \{\text{Fail,Fail,Pass}\}: \ 1/3, 2/3 \Rightarrow H \approx 0.918 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Study}) &= 0.918 - \left[\frac{3}{6}(0) + \frac{3}{6}(0.918)\right] = 0.459
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
S_{\text{Sleep=Enough}} &= \{\text{Pass,Pass,Fail,Fail}\}: \ 2/2 \Rightarrow H = 1 \\
S_{\text{Sleep=Little}} &= \{\text{Pass,Pass}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow H = 0 \\
\text{Gain}(S,\text{Sleep}) &= 0.918 - \left[\frac{4}{6}(1) + \frac{2}{6}(0)\right] = 0.251
\end{align*}$$
Since Gain(Study) $\approx 0.459 >$ Gain(Sleep) $\approx 0.251$, Study is chosen as the root.
Study = Yes is already pure (Pass). Study = No is not pure and must be split further using the only remaining attribute, Sleep:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{No, Enough} &\to \{\text{Fail,Fail}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow \text{leaf } = \text{Fail} \\
\text{No, Little} &\to \{\text{Pass}\}: \ \text{pure} \Rightarrow \text{leaf } = \text{Pass}
\end{align*}$$

\boxed{\text{Final Tree: Study} \to \{\text{Yes}: \text{Pass}, \ \text{No} \to \text{Sleep} \to \{\text{Enough}: \text{Fail}, \text{Little}: \text{Pass}\}\}}

title: ID3 Stopping Conditions (Base Cases): enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
ID3 Stopping Conditions (Base Cases):

1. All remaining examples belong to the same class $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with that class
2. No attributes are left to split on $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with the majority class
3. A branch has no matching examples $\Rightarrow$ create a leaf with the majority class of the parent set
4. Otherwise pick the attribute with the highest Information Gain and recurse

title: Bayes' Theorem
content:
Bayes' Theorem relates the probability of a hypothesis $H$ given evidence $E$ to the reverse conditional probability:
\[
P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}
\]
where $P(H)$ is the prior, $P(E \mid H)$ is the likelihood, $P(E)$ is the evidence probability, and $P(H \mid E)$ is the posterior.

This is simply the definition of conditional probability rearranged and applied in the reverse direction.

title: Example 2.13 --- Medical Test Diagnosis
content:
Given:

- $P(\text{Disease}) = 0.01$
- $P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{Disease}) = 0.9$
- $P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{NoDisease}) = 0.05$

Find $P(\text{Disease} \mid \text{Positive})$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Positive}) &= P(\text{Positive}|\text{Disease})P(\text{Disease}) + P(\text{Positive}|\text{NoDisease})P(\text{NoDisease}) \\
&= (0.9)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99) \\
&= 0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Disease}|\text{Positive}) &= \frac{0.009}{0.0585}
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{P(\text{Disease}\mid\text{Positive}) \approx 0.154}

Example 2.15 --- Predicting Rain from Cloud Cover
Naive Bayes Assumption (Conditional Independence)
content:
Given the class label $C$, the naive Bayes classifier assumes that all attributes $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ are conditionally independent of one another:
\[
P(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n \mid C) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(A_i \mid C)
\]
This means that once the class is known, each attribute's probability can be computed on its own, without needing to know the values of the other attributes.

The diagram below shows this assumption as a simple graphical model: the class $C$ independently influences each attribute, and there are no direct connections between attributes themselves.

This is the same "product of independent probabilities" idea used when multiplying probabilities of independent events.

\subsection{Naive Bayes Classification}

title: Naive Bayes Classification Rule
content:
1. Compute a score $P(C_k)\prod_{i} P(A_i \mid C_k)$ for every class $C_k$ \hfill(posterior score)
2. Predict the class with the maximum score \hfill(MAP decision rule)
3. $P(E)$ is the same for every class comparison, so it can be dropped \hfill(normalization not needed)

\[
\hat{C} = \arg\max_{C_k} \; P(C_k)\prod_{i=1}^{n} P(A_i \mid C_k)
\]

title: Naive Bayes Classifier Algorithm
content:
Input: A training set with attributes $A_1,\ldots,A_n$, a class attribute $C$, and one test instance

Output: The predicted class label for the test instance

1. For each class $C_k$, compute the prior $P(C_k) = \dfrac{\text{count}(C_k)}{\text{total examples}}$.
2. For each attribute $A_i$ and each class $C_k$, compute the likelihood $P(A_i \mid C_k)$ from the training data.
3. For the test instance, compute the score $P(C_k)\prod_i P(A_i \mid C_k)$ for every class $C_k$ using the instance's attribute values.
4. Predict the class $C_k$ with the highest score.

title: Example 2.16 --- Predicting PlayCricket
content:
| \toprule Weather | Wind | PlayCricket |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Sunny | Weak | Yes |
| Sunny | Strong | No |
| Rainy | Weak | Yes |
| Rainy | Strong | Yes |
| Sunny | Weak | Yes |
| Rainy | Strong | No |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
Classify a new instance: Weather = Sunny Wind = Strong.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Yes}) &= \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad P(\text{No}) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3} \\[4pt]
P(\text{Sunny}|\text{Yes}) &= \frac{2}{4} = 0.5, \qquad P(\text{Strong}|\text{Yes}) = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \\
P(\text{Sunny}|\text{No}) &= \frac{1}{2} = 0.5, \qquad P(\text{Strong}|\text{No}) = \frac{2}{2} = 1
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Score}(\text{Yes}) &= \frac{2}{3}(0.5)(0.25) \approx 0.0833 \\
\text{Score}(\text{No}) &= \frac{1}{3}(0.5)(1) \approx 0.1667
\end{align*}$$
Since $\text{Score}(\text{No}) > \text{Score}(\text{Yes})$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class: No}}

title: Example 2.17 --- Classifying a Fruit
content:
| \toprule Color | Size | Fruit |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Red | Large | Apple |
| Green | Small | Grape |
| Red | Small | Grape |
| Red | Large | Apple |
| Green | Small | Grape |
| Red | Large | Apple |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
Classify a new instance: Color = Red Size = Small.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Apple}) &= \frac{3}{6} = 0.5, \qquad P(\text{Grape}) = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Red}|\text{Apple}) &= \frac{3}{3} = 1, \qquad P(\text{Small}|\text{Apple}) = \frac{0}{3} = 0 \\
P(\text{Red}|\text{Grape}) &= \frac{1}{3}, \qquad P(\text{Small}|\text{Grape}) = \frac{3}{3} = 1
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Score}(\text{Apple}) &= (0.5)(1)(0) = 0 \\
\text{Score}(\text{Grape}) &= (0.5)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(1) \approx 0.1667
\end{align*}$$
Since $\text{Score}(\text{Grape}) > \text{Score}(\text{Apple})$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class: Grape}}

title: Example 2.18 --- Classifying an Email
content:
| \toprule ContainsMoney | ContainsFree | Class |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule Yes | Yes | Spam |
| Yes | No | Spam |
| No | No | NotSpam |
| No | Yes | NotSpam |
| Yes | Yes | Spam |
| No | No | NotSpam |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
Classify a new instance: ContainsMoney = Yes ContainsFree = No.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
P(\text{Spam}) &= \frac{3}{6} = 0.5, \qquad P(\text{NotSpam}) = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 \\[4pt]
P(\text{Money=Yes}|\text{Spam}) &= \frac{3}{3} = 1, \qquad P(\text{Free=No}|\text{Spam}) = \frac{1}{3} \\
P(\text{Money=Yes}|\text{NotSpam}) &= \frac{0}{3} = 0, \qquad P(\text{Free=No}|\text{NotSpam}) = \frac{2}{3}
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Score}(\text{Spam}) &= (0.5)(1)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \approx 0.1667 \\
\text{Score}(\text{NotSpam}) &= (0.5)(0)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 0
\end{align*}$$
Since $\text{Score}(\text{Spam}) > \text{Score}(\text{NotSpam})$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class: Spam}}

title: The Zero-Probability Problem: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] If an
content:
The Zero-Probability Problem:

1. If an attribute value never occurs with a class in training data, its likelihood is $0$
2. A single zero likelihood forces the entire product (and hence the score) to $0$, as seen for Apple in Example 2.17
3. This can wrongly rule out a class even when the other evidence supports it
4. Fix: Laplace smoothing adds a small count to every likelihood so no probability is ever exactly zero

title: Artificial Neural Network
content: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the brain, made of simple processing units called neurons that are connected together. Each connection carries a weight, and the network learns by adjusting these weights so that a given input produces the desired output.

title: Perceptron
content:
A perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron. It takes input values $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$, multiplies each by a weight $w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_n$, adds a bias term $b$, and passes the result through an activation function $f$ to produce the output:
\[
\text{net} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b, \qquad y = f(\text{net})
\]

This is nothing more than a dot product of the weight vector and the input vector, shifted by a constant and passed through a function.

\subsection{Activation Functions}

title: Common Activation Functions
content:
1. Step (threshold) function \hfill(hard decision)
\[
f(\text{net}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if net} \ge 0 \\ 0 & \text{if net} < 0 \end{cases}
\]
2. Sigmoid function \hfill(smooth 0 to 1 output)
\[
f(\text{net}) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\text{net}}}
\]

title: Perceptron Output Computation
content:
Input: input values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, weights $w_1,\ldots,w_n$, bias $b$, an activation function $f$

Output: the perceptron's output $y$

1. Compute the weighted sum $\text{net} = \sum_i w_i x_i + b$.
2. Apply the activation function: $y = f(\text{net})$.
3. Return $y$.

title: Example 2.19 --- Perceptron with Step Activation
content:
A perceptron has weights $w_1=0.6$, $w_2=0.6$, bias $b=-0.5$, and step activation. Compute its output for $x_1=1, x_2=0$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net} &= (0.6)(1) + (0.6)(0) + (-0.5) = 0.1 \\
y &= f(0.1) = 1 \quad (\text{since } 0.1 \ge 0)
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 1}

title: Example 2.20 --- Same Perceptron a Different Input
content:
Using the same perceptron as Example 2.19, compute the output for $x_1=0, x_2=0$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net} &= (0.6)(0) + (0.6)(0) + (-0.5) = -0.5 \\
y &= f(-0.5) = 0 \quad (\text{since } -0.5 < 0)
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 0}

title: Example 2.21 --- Same Perceptron a Third Input
content:
Using the same perceptron as Example 2.19, compute the output for $x_1=1, x_2=1$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net} &= (0.6)(1) + (0.6)(1) + (-0.5) = 0.7 \\
y &= f(0.7) = 1 \quad (\text{since } 0.7 \ge 0)
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 1}

title: Observation from Examples 2.19 to 2.21:
content:
Observation from Examples 2.19 to 2.21:

1. The output is $1$ whenever at least one input is $1$, and $0$ only when both inputs are $0$
2. This perceptron has learned the logical OR function
3. A single perceptron can only represent linearly separable functions (like AND, OR); it cannot represent XOR, which is why hidden layers are needed (Section 2.3.3)

title: Example 2.22 --- Perceptron with Sigmoid Activation
Example 2.23 --- Sigmoid Perceptron a Different Input
Example 2.24 --- Sigmoid Perceptron a Third Input
Step vs Sigmoid: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Step activation
content:
Step vs Sigmoid:

1. Step activation gives a hard $0$ or $1$ output only
2. Sigmoid activation gives a smooth value strictly between $0$ and $1$, useful as a "confidence" score
3. As net $\to +\infty$, sigmoid $\to 1$; as net $\to -\infty$, sigmoid $\to 0$

\subsection{Multilayer Neural Networks and Forward Propagation}

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
content:
A multilayer perceptron is a network with one or more hidden layers placed between the input layer and the output layer. Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer, each connection has its own weight, and information flows forward from input to output through the hidden neurons.

{\small Input Layer $\to$ Hidden Layer $\to$ Output Layer}

title: Forward Propagation Algorithm
content:
Input: input vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, weights and biases for the hidden layer and the output layer, an activation function $f$

Output: the network's final output $y$

1. For each hidden neuron $h_j$, compute $\text{net}_{h_j} = \sum_i w_{ij}x_i + b_j$ and then $h_j = f(\text{net}_{h_j})$.
2. Using the hidden outputs $h_j$ as inputs, compute $\text{net}_{y} = \sum_j v_j h_j + b_{\text{out}}$.
3. Compute the final output $y = f(\text{net}_y)$.
4. Return $y$.

title: Example 2.25 --- Forward Pass Through a Two Layer Network
content:
A network has two hidden neurons and one output neuron, all with step activation:
\[
h_1 = f(x_1+x_2-0.5), \qquad h_2 = f(x_1+x_2-1.5), \qquad y = f(h_1-h_2-0.5)
\]
Compute the output for $x_1=1, x_2=0$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net}_{h_1} &= 1+0-0.5 = 0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_1 = f(0.5) = 1 \\
\text{net}_{h_2} &= 1+0-1.5 = -0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_2 = f(-0.5) = 0 \\
\text{net}_y &= h_1-h_2-0.5 = 1-0-0.5 = 0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ y = f(0.5) = 1
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 1}

title: Example 2.26 --- Forward Pass Through the Same Network
content:
Using the same network as Example 2.25, compute the output for $x_1=1, x_2=1$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net}_{h_1} &= 1+1-0.5 = 1.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_1 = f(1.5) = 1 \\
\text{net}_{h_2} &= 1+1-1.5 = 0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_2 = f(0.5) = 1 \\
\text{net}_y &= h_1-h_2-0.5 = 1-1-0.5 = -0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ y = f(-0.5) = 0
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 0}

title: Example 2.27 --- Forward Pass Through the Same Network
content:
Using the same network as Example 2.25, compute the output for $x_1=0, x_2=0$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net}_{h_1} &= 0+0-0.5 = -0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_1 = f(-0.5) = 0 \\
\text{net}_{h_2} &= 0+0-1.5 = -1.5 \ \Rightarrow\ h_2 = f(-1.5) = 0 \\
\text{net}_y &= h_1-h_2-0.5 = 0-0-0.5 = -0.5 \ \Rightarrow\ y = f(-0.5) = 0
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{y = 0}

title: Why This Network Matters: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Checking
content:
Why This Network Matters:

1. Checking all four input combinations gives outputs $0,1,1,0$ for $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$
2. This is exactly the XOR function, which a single perceptron can never compute (see the keypoint after Example 2.21)
3. $h_1$ behaves like an OR gate and $h_2$ behaves like an AND gate; the output combines them as "$h_1$ true AND $h_2$ false"
4. This is the classic illustration of why hidden layers give neural networks more power than a single perceptron

title: Hyperplane
content:
A hyperplane is the decision boundary that separates two classes in feature space. In two dimensions it is simply a line, defined by:
\[
w \cdot x + b = 0
\]
where $w$ is the weight vector (normal to the hyperplane) and $b$ is the bias term.

title: Margin and Support Vectors
content:
The margin is the distance between the hyperplane and the closest training points from either class. The support vectors are exactly those closest points — they are the only points that determine the position of the hyperplane. The Support Vector Machine (SVM) chooses the hyperplane that makes this margin as large as possible.

This is the same idea as finding a line that keeps the maximum possible distance from the nearest point on either side, using distance formulas already familiar from coordinate geometry.

The circled points touching the dashed margin lines are the support vectors — every other point could be removed without changing the hyperplane at all.

\subsection{The SVM Decision Function}

title: Properties of the SVM Decision Function
content:
1. A point is classified using $f(x) = \text{sign}(w \cdot x + b)$ \hfill(decision rule)
2. $w \cdot x + b > 0$ places the point on the $+1$ side \hfill(positive class)
3. $w \cdot x + b < 0$ places the point on the $-1$ side \hfill(negative class)
4. $w \cdot x + b = 0$ means the point lies exactly on the hyperplane \hfill(boundary case)

title: SVM Classification Algorithm
content:
Input: weight vector $w$, bias $b$, and a test point $x$

Output: predicted class label $+1$ or $-1$ for $x$

1. Compute the dot product $w \cdot x$.
2. Add the bias: $\text{score} = w \cdot x + b$.
3. If $\text{score} > 0$ predict class $+1$; if $\text{score} < 0$ predict class $-1$; if $\text{score} = 0$ the point lies on the hyperplane.
4. Return the predicted class.

title: Example 2.28 --- Classifying a Point (Positive Side)
content:
A trained SVM has $w = (2,-1)$ and $b = -1$. Classify the point $x = (3,1)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{score} &= w \cdot x + b = (2)(3) + (-1)(1) + (-1) \\
&= 6 - 1 - 1 = 4
\end{align*}$$
Since $4 > 0$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class: } +1}

title: Example 2.29 --- Classifying a Point (Negative Side)
content:
Using the same SVM as Example 2.28 ($w=(2,-1)$, $b=-1$), classify the point $x = (0,3)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{score} &= (2)(0) + (-1)(3) + (-1) \\
&= 0 - 3 - 1 = -4
\end{align*}$$
Since $-4 < 0$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class: } -1}

title: Example 2.30 --- Classifying a Point on the Boundary
content:
Using the same SVM as Example 2.28 ($w=(2,-1)$, $b=-1$), classify the point $x = (1,1)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{score} &= (2)(1) + (-1)(1) + (-1) \\
&= 2 - 1 - 1 = 0
\end{align*}$$
Since $\text{score} = 0$, the point lies exactly on the hyperplane, so it is a support vector.\\
\boxed{x=(1,1) \text{ lies on the decision boundary}}

title: Reading the Score: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] The sign
content:
Reading the Score:

1. The sign of $w\cdot x+b$ gives the predicted class
2. The magnitude of $w\cdot x+b$ (before normalizing by $\|w\|$) hints at how far the point is from the boundary — larger magnitude means the model is more confident
3. Example 2.30 shows a point exactly on the hyperplane, which is precisely what defines a support vector

\subsection{Computing the Margin}

title: Margin Width Formula
content:
Once the SVM has found the optimal $w$, the width of the margin (distance between the two dashed boundary lines) is:
\[
\text{Margin} = \frac{2}{\|w\|}, \qquad \|w\| = \sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2 + \cdots + w_n^2}
\]

title: Distance from a Point to the Hyperplane
content:
The perpendicular distance from any point $x$ to the hyperplane $w\cdot x + b = 0$ is:
\[
d = \frac{|w \cdot x + b|}{\|w\|}
\]

This is simply the point-to-line distance formula the students already know from coordinate geometry, extended to vector notation.

title: Example 2.31 --- Margin Width for a Given Weight Vector
Example 2.32 --- Margin Width for a Simpler Weight Vector
Example 2.33 --- Distance from a Point to the Hyperplane
SVM Summary: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] A smaller $\|w\|$
content:
SVM Summary:

1. A smaller $\|w\|$ gives a larger margin — this is exactly what SVM training optimizes for
2. Only the support vectors (score $=0$ direction, i.e. the closest points) affect $w$ and $b$; all other points can change freely without moving the hyperplane
3. For data that is not linearly separable in its original features, the kernel trick maps points into a higher-dimensional space where a separating hyperplane does exist — the calculations themselves stay the same dot-product-and-sign process shown above, just in the transformed space

title: Overfitting
content: A model overfits when it fits the training data too closely including its noise and random fluctuations so that it performs very well on training data but poorly on new unseen data. In decision trees, this happens when the tree grows too many branches trying to perfectly classify every single training example.

title: Noise
content:
Noise refers to errors or random variation in the training data, such as mislabeled examples or incorrect attribute values, that do not reflect the true underlying pattern. A tree that tries to perfectly fit noisy examples ends up learning the noise itself rather than the real pattern.

The graph below shows the classic pattern: as tree size (number of nodes) increases, training error keeps falling, but test error falls only up to a point and then rises again — that turning point is where overfitting begins.

title: Example 2.34 --- Identifying the Point of Overfitting
content:
A decision tree is trained to different depths, giving the following accuracies:
| \toprule Depth | Training Accuracy | Testing Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| \midrule 2 | 70\% | 68\% |
| 4 | 85\% | 80\% |
| 6 | 95\% | 78\% |
| 8 | 99\% | 70\% |
| \bottomrule |  |  |
At which depth does the tree start to overfit?

Solution:
Training accuracy keeps rising at every depth (70\%,85\%,95\%,99\%), but testing accuracy rises only up to Depth 4 (80\%) and then falls at Depth 6 (78\%) and Depth 8 (70\%). Overfitting begins exactly where testing accuracy turns downward while training accuracy keeps climbing.
\boxed{\text{Overfitting begins after Depth 4 (i.e. from Depth 6 onward)}}

title: Example 2.35 --- Choosing the Best Depth to Stop
content:
Using the table from Example 2.34, which depth should be chosen as the final tree depth?

Solution:
The best depth is the one with the highest testing accuracy, since testing accuracy estimates performance on new data. From the table, the maximum testing accuracy is 80\% at Depth 4.
\boxed{\text{Best depth} = 4}

title: Example 2.36 --- Computing the Generalization Gap
content:
Using the table from Example 2.34, compute the generalization gap (Training Accuracy $-$ Testing Accuracy) at each depth and identify which depth is most overfit.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Depth 2:} \quad &70\%-68\% = 2\% \\
\text{Depth 4:} \quad &85\%-80\% = 5\% \\
\text{Depth 6:} \quad &95\%-78\% = 17\% \\
\text{Depth 8:} \quad &99\%-70\% = 29\%
\end{align*}$$
The gap grows steadily and is largest at Depth 8, showing the training accuracy has become disconnected from real performance.
\boxed{\text{Depth 8 is the most overfit (gap} = 29\%)}

title: Signs of Overfitting: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Training accuracy
content:
Signs of Overfitting:

1. Training accuracy is very high (often near 100\%) while testing accuracy is much lower
2. The gap between training and testing accuracy keeps growing as the model grows more complex
3. The tree has very deep branches or leaves covering only one or two training examples

\subsection{Pruning}

title: Pruning
content:
Pruning is the process of removing branches or subtrees from a decision tree that add complexity without improving (or that even hurt) accuracy on unseen data. Pre-pruning stops tree growth early using a stopping condition. Post-pruning grows the full tree first and then removes subtrees afterward, checking accuracy on a separate validation set.

This is the same "simplify the model, don't just fit every last training point" idea behind avoiding an unnecessarily high-degree curve fit in regression.

title: Reduced Error Pruning
content:
Input: a fully grown decision tree $T$, a validation dataset $V$ separate from the training data

Output: a pruned decision tree $T'$

1. Compute the accuracy of $T$ on $V$.
2. For each internal node $n$ (starting near the leaves and working upward), temporarily replace the subtree rooted at $n$ with a leaf labeled by the majority class of the training examples reaching $n$.
3. Evaluate the accuracy of this modified tree on $V$.
4. If the accuracy on $V$ does not decrease, keep the replacement permanently (prune the subtree); otherwise restore the original subtree.
5. Repeat steps 2 to 4 for every internal node until no further pruning improves or maintains validation accuracy.
6. Return the final pruned tree $T'$.

title: Example 2.37 --- Deciding Whether to Prune (Accuracy Improves)
content:
Before pruning a subtree at node $X$, validation accuracy is 82\%. After replacing the subtree at $X$ with a leaf, validation accuracy becomes 85\%. Should node $X$'s subtree be pruned?

Solution:
Compare accuracies: $85\% > 82\%$, so accuracy does not decrease after pruning; in fact it improves.
\boxed{\text{Yes, prune the subtree at } X}

title: Example 2.38 --- Deciding Whether to Prune (Accuracy Drops)
content:
Before pruning a subtree at node $Y$, validation accuracy is 90\%. After replacing the subtree at $Y$ with a leaf, validation accuracy becomes 88\%. Should node $Y$'s subtree be pruned?

Solution:
Compare accuracies: $88\% < 90\%$, so accuracy decreases after pruning.
\boxed{\text{No, keep the subtree at } Y}

title: Example 2.39 --- Deciding Whether to Prune (Accuracy Unchanged)
content:
Before pruning a subtree at node $Z$, validation accuracy is 78\%. After replacing the subtree at $Z$ with a leaf, validation accuracy remains 78\%. Should node $Z$'s subtree be pruned?

Solution:
Compare accuracies: $78\% = 78\%$, accuracy does not decrease. Reduced Error Pruning prefers the simpler tree whenever accuracy does not get worse.
\boxed{\text{Yes, prune the subtree at } Z}

title: Pre-Pruning vs Post-Pruning: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Pre-pruning is
content:
Pre-Pruning vs Post-Pruning:

1. Pre-pruning is faster since the tree never grows too large, but risks stopping too early (underfitting)
2. Post-pruning is more reliable since it evaluates the effect of removing each subtree directly on validation data
3. Pruning always trades a small amount of training accuracy for better generalization to new data

title: Confusion Matrix
content:
A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes a classifier's predictions against the true labels for a binary classification problem. It has four counts: True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), False Negatives (FN), and True Negatives (TN).

| \toprule |  | \multicolumn{2}{c}{Actual} |  |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  | Positive | Negative |
| \midrule \multirow{2}{*}{Predicted} | Positive | TP | FP |
|  | Negative | FN | TN |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |

\subsection{Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score}

title: Classifier Evaluation Metrics
content:
1. $\text{Accuracy} = \dfrac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$ \hfill(overall correctness)
2. $\text{Precision} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}$ \hfill(of predicted positives, how many were right)
3. $\text{Recall} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$ \hfill(of actual positives, how many were found)
4. $\text{F1-score} = \dfrac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}$ \hfill(harmonic mean of Precision and Recall)

title: Computing Classifier Metrics
content:
Input: confusion matrix counts $TP$, $FP$, $FN$, $TN$

Output: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score

1. Compute $\text{Accuracy} = \dfrac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$.
2. Compute $\text{Precision} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}$.
3. Compute $\text{Recall} = \dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$.
4. Compute $\text{F1-score} = \dfrac{2\times\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}$.
5. Return all four values.

title: Example 2.40 --- Metrics from a Balanced Confusion Matrix
content:
A classifier gives the confusion matrix below.
| \toprule |  | \multicolumn{2}{c}{Actual} |  |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  | Positive | Negative |
| \midrule \multirow{2}{*}{Predicted} | Positive | 40 | 10 |
|  | Negative | 5 | 45 |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |
Compute Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Accuracy} &= \frac{40+45}{40+45+10+5} = \frac{85}{100} = 0.85 \\
\text{Precision} &= \frac{40}{40+10} = \frac{40}{50} = 0.8 \\
\text{Recall} &= \frac{40}{40+5} = \frac{40}{45} \approx 0.889 \\
\text{F1} &= \frac{2(0.8)(0.889)}{0.8+0.889} = \frac{1.422}{1.689}
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Accuracy}=0.85,\ \text{Precision}=0.8,\ \text{Recall}\approx0.889,\ F1\approx0.842}

title: Example 2.41 --- Metrics from a Small Balanced Matrix
content:
A classifier gives the confusion matrix below.
| \toprule |  | \multicolumn{2}{c}{Actual} |  |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  | Positive | Negative |
| \midrule \multirow{2}{*}{Predicted} | Positive | 8 | 2 |
|  | Negative | 2 | 8 |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |
Compute Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Accuracy} &= \frac{8+8}{8+8+2+2} = \frac{16}{20} = 0.8 \\
\text{Precision} &= \frac{8}{8+2} = 0.8 \\
\text{Recall} &= \frac{8}{8+2} = 0.8 \\
\text{F1} &= \frac{2(0.8)(0.8)}{0.8+0.8} = \frac{1.28}{1.6}
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Accuracy}=\text{Precision}=\text{Recall}=F1=0.8}

title: Example 2.42 --- Metrics from an Imbalanced Confusion Matrix
content:
A classifier gives the confusion matrix below.
| \toprule |  | \multicolumn{2}{c}{Actual} |  |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  | Positive | Negative |
| \midrule \multirow{2}{*}{Predicted} | Positive | 5 | 15 |
|  | Negative | 0 | 80 |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |
Compute Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Accuracy} &= \frac{5+80}{5+80+15+0} = \frac{85}{100} = 0.85 \\
\text{Precision} &= \frac{5}{5+15} = \frac{5}{20} = 0.25 \\
\text{Recall} &= \frac{5}{5+0} = \frac{5}{5} = 1.0 \\
\text{F1} &= \frac{2(0.25)(1.0)}{0.25+1.0} = \frac{0.5}{1.25}
\end{align*}$$
\boxed{\text{Accuracy}=0.85,\ \text{Precision}=0.25,\ \text{Recall}=1.0,\ F1=0.4}
Although accuracy looks high (85\%), the very low precision reveals the classifier is predicting "Positive" far too often — this is exactly why accuracy alone can be misleading. ✓

title: Choosing the Right Metric: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Accuracy
content:
Choosing the Right Metric:

1. Accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced, as seen in Example 2.42
2. Precision matters most when false positives are costly (e.g. spam filtering)
3. Recall matters most when false negatives are costly (e.g. disease detection)
4. F1-score is used when a single balance between Precision and Recall is needed

title: Linear Regression
content:
Linear regression models the relationship between one input attribute $x$ and a continuous output $y$ by fitting a straight line:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x
\]
where $b_1$ is the slope (how much $y$ changes per unit change in $x$) and $b_0$ is the intercept (the predicted value when $x=0$).

title: Least Squares Method
content:
The best-fitting line is the one that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the actual values $y_i$ and the predicted values $\hat{y}_i$. The coefficients that achieve this minimum are:
\[
b_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}
\]
where $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ are the means of the $x$ and $y$ values.

This is the same mean-and-deviation idea used when computing variance, just applied to two variables together instead of one.

title: Simple Linear Regression (Least Squares)
content:
Input: training points $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)$, and a new value $x_{\text{new}}$ to predict

Output: coefficients $b_0$, $b_1$, and the predicted value $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$

1. Compute the means $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i$.
2. Compute $\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})$ and $\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2$.
3. Compute the slope $b_1 = \dfrac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2}$.
4. Compute the intercept $b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}$.
5. Form the regression equation $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$.
6. Substitute $x_{\text{new}}$ into the equation to get $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$.

title: Example 2.43 --- Predicting Exam Score from Study Hours
content:
| \toprule Hours Studied ($x$) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Score /10 ($y$) | 2 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 6 |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |  |  |
Find the regression line and predict the score for a student who studies 6 hours.

Solution:
\begin{align*}
\bar{x} &= \frac{1+2+3+4+5}{5} = 3, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{2+3+5+4+6}{5} = 4 \\[4pt]
\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}) &= (-2)(-2)+(-1)(-1)+(0)(1)+(1)(0)+(2)(2) = 4+1+0+0+4 = 9 \\
\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 &= 4+1+0+1+4 = 10 \\[4pt]
b_1 &= \frac{9}{10} = 0.9, \qquad b_0 = 4-(0.9)(3) = 1.3
\end{align*}
\[
\hat{y} = 1.3 + 0.9x
\]
Predicting for $x=6$: $\hat{y} = 1.3+0.9(6) = 1.3+5.4$
\boxed{\hat{y}(6) = 6.7}

title: Example 2.44 --- Predicting Sales from Advertising Spend
Example 2.45 --- Predicting Plant Height Growth
content:
| \toprule Weeks Grown ($x$) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Height Growth cm ($y$) | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| \bottomrule |  |  |  |  |
Find the regression line and predict the growth after 5 weeks.

Solution:
\begin{align*}
\bar{x} &= \frac{1+2+3+4}{4} = 2.5, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{1+2+2+3}{4} = 2 \\[4pt]
\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}) &= (-1.5)(-1)+(-0.5)(0)+(0.5)(0)+(1.5)(1) = 1.5+0+0+1.5 = 3 \\
\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 &= 2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25 = 5 \\[4pt]
b_1 &= \frac{3}{5} = 0.6, \qquad b_0 = 2-(0.6)(2.5) = 0.5
\end{align*}
\[
\hat{y} = 0.5 + 0.6x
\]
Predicting for $x=5$: $\hat{y} = 0.5+0.6(5) = 0.5+3$
\boxed{\hat{y}(5) = 3.5}

title: Reading a Regression Line: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] $b_1$
content:
Reading a Regression Line:

1. $b_1$ (slope) tells us how much $y$ increases for every one-unit increase in $x$
2. $b_0$ (intercept) is only meaningful as the predicted $y$ when $x=0$
3. Predictions far outside the range of the original $x$ values (extrapolation) are less reliable

title: Logistic Regression
Logistic Regression Decision Rule
content:
1. If $P(y=1\mid x) \ge 0.5$ predict class $1$ otherwise predict class $0$ \hfill(threshold rule)
2. $P(y=1\mid x) \ge 0.5$ is equivalent to $\text{net}=w\cdot x+b \ge 0$ \hfill(shortcut check)
3. The decision boundary is the hyperplane $w\cdot x+b=0$ \hfill(same linear boundary idea as SVM)

title: Logistic Regression Classification
content:
Input: weights $w$, bias $b$, a test point $x$, decision threshold (default $0.5$)

Output: predicted class label ($0$ or $1$) and probability $P$

1. Compute $\text{net} = w\cdot x + b$.
2. Compute $P = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\text{net}}}$.
3. If $P \ge 0.5$ predict class $1$; otherwise predict class $0$.
4. Return the predicted class and $P$.

title: Example 2.48 --- Logistic Regression Prediction (Net Zero)
content:
A model has $w=(1,-1)$, $b=0$. Classify $x=(2,2)$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\text{net} &= (1)(2)+(-1)(2)+0 = 2-2 = 0 \\
P &= \frac{1}{1+e^{0}} = \frac{1}{1+1} = 0.5
\end{align*}$$
Since $P = 0.5$ meets the threshold $\ge 0.5$:
\boxed{\text{Predicted class} = 1 \ (\text{point lies exactly on the decision boundary})}

title: Linear Regression vs Logistic Regression: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
Linear Regression vs Logistic Regression:

1. Linear regression predicts a continuous value directly as $b_0+b_1x$
2. Logistic regression predicts a probability between $0$ and $1$ by passing $w\cdot x+b$ through the sigmoid function
3. Both are built from the same linear combination of attributes; only the final step (identity vs sigmoid) differs
4. Logistic regression is used for classification, not for predicting numeric quantities
